topic-000-a-circular-argument-does-rope-.title: Spatial Perception & Physical Representations
topic-000-a-circular-argument-does-rope-.overview: How can a model recover useful structure from observations that change with viewpoint, motion, or measurement? This cluster connects early accounts of sensory processing with learned depth, surfaces, shapes, and physical dynamics. Its common thread is representation: choosing coordinates, comparisons, or latent states that preserve the properties a task needs. Some papers model biological perception; others build reconstruction and simulation tools, so neighboring papers need not solve the same problem.
topic-000-a-circular-argument-does-rope-.whyItMatters: A useful physical representation can turn noisy images or sensor readings into quantities that support reconstruction, interaction, and prediction. The challenge is retaining geometry without spending unnecessary memory or confusing visual similarity with physical consistency.
topic-000-a-circular-argument-does-rope-.evolution: The sampled work moves from sensory-control and perceptual-grouping models in the late 1980s and 1990s to ordinal image codes and manifold-based reconstruction in the 2000s. Later papers emphasize learned 3D representations, human–object interactions, and simulation. Recent examples use local coordinate frames for compact surfaces and intermediate flow trajectories for inverse problems; these are connections within this sample, not a complete history.
openQuestions: Which representations retain the geometry needed for a new viewpoint or task?
How can reconstruction quality, physical consistency, and memory cost be assessed together?
When does a biologically motivated representation offer an advantage over a task-specific learned one?

topic-001-convolutional-sequence-to-sequ.title: Sequence Models & Efficient Architectures
topic-001-convolutional-sequence-to-sequ.overview: Sequence models must preserve useful dependencies across time or position while keeping training and generation affordable. This cluster spans recurrent, convolutional, attention-based, and diffusion-based designs, together with methods that reduce the cost of their underlying computations. Applications include language, speech, event prediction, time series, and streaming video. An architectural improvement and a faster implementation address different bottlenecks, even when both make long sequences easier to handle.
topic-001-convolutional-sequence-to-sequ.whyItMatters: Latency, memory traffic, and context length determine whether a strong sequence model is usable. Understanding these bottlenecks helps explain why quality improvements and speedups must be evaluated separately.
topic-001-convolutional-sequence-to-sequ.evolution: Early sampled papers address temporal invariance and real-time harmony. In 2017, convolutional sequence-to-sequence learning and attention-centered architectures offer different alternatives to recurrence. The sample then expands toward efficient attention, multiscale byte modeling, and cache-aware inference. Recent work studies in-context behavior, parallel diffusion decoding, and streaming generation, linking model design to the scheduling of computation.
openQuestions: Which long-range dependencies survive compression or sparse attention?
How do training throughput, first-token latency, and sustained generation speed trade off?
When can parallel generation retain temporal coherence and output quality?

topic-002-quest-query-aware-sparsity-for.title: Language Models, Reasoning & Agents
topic-002-quest-query-aware-sparsity-for.overview: This cluster follows how language representations support retrieval, reasoning, tool use, and interaction. Alongside techniques that improve capability are studies of what benchmarks measure, whether explanations reveal internal computation, and how an agent interprets a user's intent. The papers treat a language model both as a predictor of text and as one component in a larger decision process involving context, tools, evaluators, and people.
topic-002-quest-query-aware-sparsity-for.whyItMatters: A useful language system must retrieve relevant information, spend computation where it helps, and produce answers whose apparent fluency matches their reliability. Agent settings add questions about clarification, tool coordination, and trustworthy evaluation.
topic-002-quest-query-aware-sparsity-for.evolution: Word Space provides an early example of corpus-derived semantic representations. The sampled 2020s work includes retrieval-augmented generation, preference training, specialized code and domain models, and long-context methods. More recent papers explore routing among models, latent reasoning, clarification, and activation-based explanations. Benchmark contamination and agent-security studies develop alongside these capability improvements rather than constituting evidence that the systems are already reliable.
openQuestions: How can evaluations distinguish genuine reasoning from memorization or benchmark leakage?
When do internal-state explanations reveal information unavailable from the input alone?
How should an agent balance clarification, retrieval, extra computation, and acting on an answer?

topic-003-canonical-tensor-decomposition.title: Structured Learning & Data Efficiency
topic-003-canonical-tensor-decomposition.overview: Many datasets contain useful structure across variables, tasks, sources, or time. This cluster brings together methods that exploit that structure: tensor factorization for missing facts, multiple expert views for clustering, structured regression, and approaches to continual or multi-source learning. It also includes computational strategies for sharing resources across learners. The collection is broad; its unifying question is how to extract more useful learning from limited data or compute.
topic-003-canonical-tensor-decomposition.whyItMatters: Ignoring relationships can waste supervision, while imposing the wrong structure can introduce bias. The papers offer different ways to share information and computation without assuming that every task or source is identical.
topic-003-canonical-tensor-decomposition.evolution: The sample begins with large-scale transductive learning and develops through multi-output prediction, structured regression, and knowledge-base factorization. Later work studies continual learning, learned equations, data generation, and uncertainty across shifted sources. Recent systems work examines low-rank adaptation, federated synthetic data, and balancing expert computation. These branches share resource constraints but do not form a single sequential algorithmic lineage.
openQuestions: When does sharing information between tasks or sources help rather than bias the learner?
How can useful structure be learned when prior assumptions are uncertain?
Which gains survive when memory, communication, and uncertainty quality are counted together?

topic-004-reinforcement-learning-with-pr.title: Reinforcement Learning & Control
topic-004-reinforcement-learning-with-pr.overview: Reinforcement learning studies how actions should change in response to rewards and experience. This cluster covers continuous control, actor–critic methods, goal decomposition, imitation, human feedback, and cooperation among agents. A recurring issue is how to assign credit across a trajectory: a useful action may pay off only much later, and exploratory actions may be costly. Several papers also examine how representations and curricula make learning easier.
topic-004-reinforcement-learning-with-pr.whyItMatters: Control and interactive assistance require more than predicting a label: actions change what happens next. Reliable learning therefore depends on exploration, feedback quality, and behavior outside the training situations.
topic-004-reinforcement-learning-with-pr.evolution: Early sampled work examines muscle-driven control and reuse of simpler task sequences. Later papers introduce continuous-action sampling, preference feedback, sub-goal trees, and offline imitation. Work on compositional curricula connects these themes to shaping in animals. Recent entries extend trajectory learning to language-model reasoning and multi-turn agents, while evolution-strategy studies explore a different route to reward-guided model tuning.
openQuestions: How can an agent explore efficiently without wasting long or risky interactions?
Which subskills and representations transfer to new goals?
How can learning from demonstrations or preferences remain reliable when the feedback is incomplete?

topic-005-bridging-the-gap-between-avera.title: Decisions under Constraints & Partial Information
topic-005-bridging-the-gap-between-avera.overview: The papers in this cluster ask how to make decisions when rewards are only one part of the problem. An agent may face hidden state, unfamiliar partners, long-term constraints, limited communication, or a choice of how to value future rewards. Information itself can be useful: gathering evidence about the world or another player can improve later decisions. The cluster also includes neighboring work on private and distributed learning constraints.
topic-005-bridging-the-gap-between-avera.whyItMatters: A policy that maximizes an unconstrained score may be unusable when resources, information, or permissible actions are restricted. Explicitly modeling these conditions makes it possible to state what a guarantee actually covers.
topic-005-bridging-the-gap-between-avera.evolution: The sampled papers move through private learning, information-seeking POMDP planning, and evaluation of policies from existing data. Subsequent work addresses team games, constrained Markov decision processes, and adaptation to unknown peers. A recent analysis of average-reward temporal-difference learning revisits a basic difficulty: guarantees from discounted problems do not automatically transfer when the underlying operator loses its contraction property.
openQuestions: How should the value of information be balanced against immediate reward?
Which guarantees survive partial observation and changing partners?
Can average-reward and constrained learning retain tractable convergence guarantees in practical function approximators?

topic-006-pocket2mol-efficient-molecular.title: Graph Learning & Relational Structure
topic-006-pocket2mol-efficient-molecular.overview: Graphs represent entities together with their relationships, but the right graph and the right computation over it depend on the task. This cluster spans inference in graphical models, discovering networks, graph generation, and neural message passing. Applications include molecules, biological interactions, brain networks, and relational databases. Several papers challenge fixed design choices, such as using one geometry for every neighborhood or treating a database schema as an unchangeable graph.
topic-006-pocket2mol-efficient-molecular.whyItMatters: Relations often contain information absent from individual features. At the same time, poorly chosen edges or propagation rules can obscure that information, so representation design and inference must be considered together.
topic-006-pocket2mol-efficient-molecular.evolution: The sample connects early constraint-network computation and belief propagation with hierarchical probabilistic models and graph-structure estimation. Later work develops graph neural networks and molecular generation conditioned on three-dimensional protein pockets. Recent studies revisit initialization, dynamic curvature, alternatives to message passing in correlation-based brain graphs, and learnable graph construction for relational databases.
openQuestions: When should graph structure be learned instead of fixed in advance?
How can a model adapt to heterogeneous relationships and changing topology?
Which graph-generation metrics reflect the downstream usefulness of a proposed structure?

topic-007-concentration-bounds-for-cvar-.title: Online Learning, Bandits & Risk
topic-007-concentration-bounds-for-cvar-.overview: An online learner acts before it knows all the consequences and updates its choices as feedback arrives. This cluster includes selecting the best option, ranking items, caching, pricing, matching, and scheduling. Bandit feedback reveals only what happened for chosen actions, making exploration essential. Other papers study confidence and tail risk, asking how to compare decisions when rare poor outcomes matter as well as average performance.
topic-007-concentration-bounds-for-cvar-.whyItMatters: A good adaptive decision rule must account for the cost of learning, the possibility of environmental change, and the consequences of uncertainty. Regret and identification cost offer different ways to formalize these tradeoffs.
topic-007-concentration-bounds-for-cvar-.evolution: Adaptive caching illustrates early practical use of online policy selection in this sample. Later work develops sequential candidate selection, ranking bandits, and identification with risk-sensitive or lower-cost approximate feedback. More recent entries address stochastic–adversarial adaptation, model-risk comparison, delayed choices, decentralized markets, and packet deadlines. Each application changes which feedback and timing assumptions are realistic.
openQuestions: How much exploration is worthwhile when feedback is expensive or delayed?
Can one method exploit stable conditions while remaining robust to adversarial changes?
How should tail risk or deadlines change the objective used to compare decisions?

topic-008-automated-synthetic-to-real-ge.title: Vision–Language Learning & Visual Generation
topic-008-automated-synthetic-to-real-ge.overview: This cluster links understanding visual content with generating it under useful control. It includes image recognition, domain transfer, vision–language models, visual datasets, and diffusion-based images, avatars, and videos. A recurring challenge is alignment: a model must connect words, image evidence, spatial structure, and requested behavior without letting one source dominate incorrectly. Some papers improve representations, while others design tasks that expose their failures.
topic-008-automated-synthetic-to-real-ge.whyItMatters: Visual fluency is not enough for a system that must reason about objects or follow an editing instruction. Transfer, controllability, and spatial consistency determine whether a model remains useful beyond familiar benchmark images.
topic-008-automated-synthetic-to-real-ge.evolution: The sample starts with visual attention and scene understanding, then expands to image–language tasks and domain transfer. In the 2020s, large visual datasets, instruction-tuned multimodal models, and diffusion generation become prominent. Recent examples emphasize controlled motion, world modeling, and active use of geometry. These additions complement rather than eliminate older problems of bias, uncertainty, and generalization.
openQuestions: How can generated content follow instructions while preserving identity, geometry, and temporal consistency?
When does a model use visual evidence instead of language-based shortcuts?
Which evaluations reveal failures under new domains, objects, and interaction patterns?

topic-009-how-to-escape-saddle-points-ef.title: Optimization & Efficient Estimation
topic-009-how-to-escape-saddle-points-ef.overview: Learning often reduces to finding useful parameters with limited computation, noisy measurements, or difficult objective geometry. This cluster studies sparse and low-rank estimation, saddle points, adaptive step sizes, variance reduction, and structured optimization. It also includes techniques that make computation or quantization more efficient. The shared emphasis is on making an algorithm's cost and accuracy understandable under explicit assumptions.
topic-009-how-to-escape-saddle-points-ef.whyItMatters: A mathematically valid objective is only useful when it can be optimized with realistic data, time, memory, and communication. Upper and lower bounds help distinguish an algorithmic improvement from a limitation of the problem itself.
topic-009-how-to-escape-saddle-points-ef.evolution: Early sampled work seeks efficient sparse representations and large-margin classifiers. Later papers analyze nonconvex landscapes, stochastic and asynchronous updates, and noisy submodular objectives. More recent work extends adaptivity to unknown smoothness and noise, variance reduction to curved spaces, and spectral or transform methods to dimension estimation and low-bit models. The assumptions differ across these settings and should travel with each guarantee.
openQuestions: How can an optimizer adapt to unknown noise and local geometry without costly tuning?
When do computational shortcuts preserve the statistical objective?
Which lower bounds reflect practical bottlenecks rather than an overly restrictive model of computation?

topic-010-poem-out-of-distribution-detec.title: Robustness, Security & Responsible Evaluation
topic-010-poem-out-of-distribution-detec.overview: This cluster examines failures that ordinary predictive accuracy can miss: unfamiliar inputs, mislabeled data, unfair outcomes, privacy leakage, backdoors, adversarial perturbations, and misuse of generated media. It also includes generative and uncertainty-modeling tools that support these investigations. The papers study different kinds of risk; improving one metric does not establish broad safety or fairness.
topic-010-poem-out-of-distribution-detec.whyItMatters: Deployment exposes models to inputs and incentives that differ from training. Useful evaluation needs an explicit threat or failure model and metrics connected to the people affected, as well as tests of technical performance.
topic-010-poem-out-of-distribution-detec.evolution: The sample includes adversarial generative modeling and later work on uncertainty, biased data, and out-of-distribution detection. Subsequent papers test reconstruction of training examples, model theft, backdoors, transferable perturbations, and watermarking. Privacy-comparison work questions single-number summaries, while a recent position paper argues that authenticity detection alone can miss harms to subjects of generated intimate imagery.
openQuestions: Which failures remain hidden behind aggregate accuracy or a single privacy parameter?
How well do defenses transfer to unfamiliar attacks and data distributions?
Do evaluation metrics measure the relevant harm, or only an easier technical proxy?

topic-011-the-loss-surface-of-deep-and-w.title: Generalization & Learning Theory
topic-011-the-loss-surface-of-deep-and-w.overview: Why does a trained model perform well on examples it has not seen? This cluster approaches that question through sample complexity, model expressivity, kernel methods, optimization dynamics, label noise, and distribution shift. A central theme is the gap between worst-case guarantees and the behavior of large trained networks. The papers supply different pieces of an explanation rather than one universal law of successful learning.
topic-011-the-loss-surface-of-deep-and-w.whyItMatters: Theory clarifies which claims depend on data structure, architecture, initialization, or training regime. These distinctions help avoid treating a proof for an idealized model as a guarantee for every deployed network.
topic-011-the-loss-surface-of-deep-and-w.evolution: Early sampled work studies dimensionality, depth, and sample requirements. Kernel and infinite-network analyses then offer tractable ways to examine complexity and generalization. Later work investigates exact fitting, spectral bias, random features, and mean-field limits. Recent entries connect these questions to scaling, pruning, transfer, and nonsmooth optimization, preserving an ongoing tension between idealized analysis and finite-model behavior.
openQuestions: Which bounds explain the performance of interpolating or heavily overparameterized models?
When do infinite-width or simplified-architecture predictions remain accurate at practical scale?
How do optimization choices interact with distribution shift and limited supervision?

topic-012-characterizing-and-learning-eq.title: Probabilistic Models, Causality & Scientific Inference
topic-012-characterizing-and-learning-eq.overview: This cluster uses latent variables and probabilistic structure to infer what observations do not reveal directly. It includes Gaussian processes, Bayesian sampling, change detection, causal discovery, and scientific dynamics. Recent generative models add flexible tools for simulation and uncertainty. A key distinction is between predicting an observation, recovering a hidden mechanism, and identifying a causal effect; these goals require different assumptions and evidence.
topic-012-characterizing-and-learning-eq.whyItMatters: Scientific and decision-making tasks often need uncertainty about a quantity or mechanism, not just a point prediction. Careful modeling can combine incomplete evidence while making clear which conclusions are identifiable.
topic-012-characterizing-and-learning-eq.evolution: The sample begins with neural models of physiological dynamics, hidden causes, and chemical guidance. Bayesian active learning, Gaussian-process sampling, and human change-detection models broaden the inference toolkit. Later work studies interventions, causal representations, and combining experiments across populations. Recent diffusion-based scientific models and predictive-rule-based posterior methods explore new ways to represent complex distributions and uncertainty.
openQuestions: Which latent or causal quantities can be identified from the available observations and interventions?
How can uncertainty remain calibrated when a flexible learned model replaces an explicit likelihood?
When does a scientifically useful explanation survive a change of population or experimental setting?
